\section[ilā l-ghad]{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد} (ilā l-ghad) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} the same ilā again}

\label{lesson:AR-C24-ila-al-ghad}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You already have the pattern: \textbf{ilā} + a future point = \textquotedblleft{}see you {[}then{]}.\textquotedblright{} Here it is again, with \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} filling the slot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The two pieces, one already familiar}
\textbf{\ar{إلى} \ar{الغد}} (\emph{ilā l-ghad}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{until tomorrow}\textquotedblright{}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{إلى}} (\emph{ilā}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{until},\textquotedblright{} the exact same word from \emph{ilā l-liqāʾ} (\textquotedblleft{}see you {[}later{]}\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{\ar{الغد}} (\emph{al-ghad}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow},\textquotedblright{} root \textbf{gh-d-w} (\ar{غ}-\ar{د}-\ar{و}).
  \item Note \textbf{\ar{ل}} is a sun letter, so \emph{al-ghad} would assimilate — but \textbf{\ar{غ}} (\emph{ghayn}) is a \textbf{moon letter}, so here the \emph{l} stays put: \emph{al-ghad}, not doubled the way \emph{al-liqāʾ} and \emph{as-salāma} were.
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Gh-d-w}'s core sense is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to go out at dawn, early morning}\textquotedblright{} — and \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}} grows directly out of that \textquotedblleft{}early morning\textquotedblright{} sense. This is \textbf{not} a one-off coincidence: you've already seen this \textbf{exact} shift happen in Latin, where \emph{māne} (\textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) became French's \emph{demain} and Spanish's \emph{mañana} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}). Two completely unrelated language families — Semitic and Indo-European — independently building \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} out of \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}ilā l-ghad\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}until tomorrow\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the reused piece — ilā, already known from ilā l-liqāʾ{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the root echo — gh-d-w, \textquotedblleft{}dawn/morning\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} the same shift as Latin māne $\to$ mañana/demain{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What word does \textbf{ilā l-ghad} share with \textbf{ilā l-liqāʾ}? (\textbf{Ilā}, \textquotedblleft{}until.\textquotedblright{}) What does the root \textbf{gh-d-w} literally mean, before it comes to mean \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}To go out at dawn, early morning.\textquotedblright{}}) Is this morning-to-tomorrow shift unique to Arabic? (\textbf{No} — Latin's \emph{māne} (\textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) independently became French's \emph{demain} and Spanish's \emph{mañana}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} the same way.)
\end{tcolorbox}
